cues.text: A Council Called for Reform
In November 1095, Pope Urban II , a former Cluniac monk, convened a council at Clermont in south-central France.

Continuing the reforming work of Gregory VII, he ostensibly sought to address ordinary matters of Church discipline: simony, clerical marriage, and King Philip I of France’s excommunication for an irregular marriage.

The council's twenty-eight disciplinary canons addressed these concerns in the routine manner of a regional synod — but Urban had a further, far more consequential purpose in mind for the council's final day.
An Appeal from Byzantium
Earlier that same year, envoys from the Byzantine Emperor Alexius I Comnenus had appealed to Urban for military assistance.
The appeal concerned the advancing Seljuk Turks, who had overrun most of Byzantine Anatolia in the decades since their victory at Manzikert in 1071.
Urban had already begun soliciting support for such an expedition at an earlier council in Piacenza, and Clermont offered him the opportunity to make a far more public and dramatic appeal.
The Sermon in the Open Field

On November 27, 1095, unable to fit the assembled crowd inside any building, Urban addressed them in an open field outside the city, delivering what would become one of the most consequential speeches in Church history.
Though no verbatim transcript survives—five differing chronicler accounts remain—his message combined an appeal to defend the Eastern Christians.
It also urged recovering Jerusalem’s holy places from Muslim rule, while offering a plenary indulgence to those undertaking the journey out of genuine devotion.
"God Wills It"
The crowd's response, tradition holds, was the spontaneous cry Deus vult — "God wills it" — a phrase that became the rallying cry of the movement Urban's sermon had just launched.
Word spread with extraordinary speed across Western Christendom in the months that followed.
Bishops, popular preachers such as Peter the Hermit, and Urban's own subsequent preaching tour through France carried the message.
Within less than a year of the council's close, tens of thousands of knights, peasants, and clergy took up the cross.
Legacy
The armies Clermont set in motion would go on to capture Jerusalem in July 1099, launching the two-century movement of the Crusades and establishing the Crusader States of Outremer.
No council of the medieval Church set more history in motion with a single sermon than Clermont.
Its ordinary business of disciplinary reform has been almost entirely eclipsed in historical memory.
A crowd of French bishops, knights, and pilgrims is said to have shouted four words back at their pope in an open field on a November afternoon.
